It appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Exodus, from Exodus 31:6 through Exodus 38:23. The name is associated with passages involving commands and giving, but its precise role in any particular verse requires the surrounding verse text. Its consistent rendering identifies it as a person’s name, not a general description or action.

This word means “if” and functions as a conditional conjunction, introducing a circumstance or condition connected to what follows. It does not describe a person, object, or action by itself; instead, it helps frame a statement as dependent on a particular condition. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 12:2. Its precise force in that verse belongs to the surrounding wording and sentence structure.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. The available information does not provide an explicit definition, approved meaning term, or English rendering for this Hebrew word. Its sense must therefore be determined by reading that verse together with its surrounding passage, rather than by assigning an unsupported synonym.

This Hebrew noun means “noise,” functioning as a name for what is heard. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 14:11. Because the word appears only there and the verse text is not included here, its broader shades cannot be established from this information alone. Its basic sense remains a spoken noun for noise, while the surrounding passage determines its precise force.

This Hebrew verb describes acting “proudly”—going ahead with one’s own will instead of humbly submitting to rightful authority. It portrays deliberate self-assertion, especially when a person speaks or acts as though personal desire can override God’s command. The word occurs 10 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, describing conduct that is bold and defiant rather than quiet or submissive. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew verb means "cry"—to call out loudly, especially in response to distress, danger, need, or urgent concern. It can describe an individual’s appeal or a collective outcry. The word occurs 73 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it has a broad ordinary use rather than referring to one isolated kind of cry. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on who is calling out and what prompts the call. Scripture also connects this action with people appealing in their circumstances and with God’s people calling out to him.

In Habakkuk, it is connected with an event described in terms of giving, while still functioning as the object affected by other actions.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to changes—things that are altered, exchanged, or varied. It names a change or set of changes rather than describing the act of changing. This Hebrew verb means “troubled”: it describes being disturbed, distressed, or thrown into turmoil. In the Old Testament, it occurs seven times, including descriptions of people overwhelmed by anguish and waters stirred by upheaval. As a verb, it expresses an action or condition affecting someone or something rather than naming a person, object, or quality. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word describes searching carefully or examining something to discover what is true or present. Its approved meaning is “search,” and its uses can refer to people investigating a matter, testing what is known, or examining something closely. It occurs 27 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in contexts that involve looking into reports, circumstances, or things that need to be understood. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being searched and how the action applies there.

This Hebrew verb means “hold.” It expresses an action of stopping, restraining, or keeping something from proceeding. In the Old Testament, it occurs 16 times, so its precise force depends on what is being held and the surrounding sentence. The word can function as an instruction, urging someone to hold, or as a description of something being held. Its repeated use in commands makes the basic idea especially clear: a person is told to hold rather than continue or act immediately.

This Hebrew noun refers to “espousals,” describing a formal marriage-related state or occasion. It functions as a name for that arrangement rather than as an action or description of a person. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Song of Solomon 3:11. Because it appears only there and no surrounding verse text is provided here, its precise force in that sentence depends on the passage itself; its basic sense remains “espousals.”

“Ahiramites” is a group name referring to people identified as Ahiramites. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Numbers 26:38, and functions as a plural designation rather than a description of an action or quality. The word’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical role is to identify a people or family group by this name.

Its precise significance as a name is not defined further in the available biblical evidence.

“Jahleelites” is a plural group name identifying people known by that designation. It functions as a people-name rather than a description of an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Numbers 26:26, and the same rendering is preserved in both recorded English renderings. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies a particular group of people.

This Hebrew verb means “came.” It states that a person or thing came, serving as the action word in a sentence. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both occurrences appearing in 2 Chronicles 32:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic function is to express coming as an action. It should therefore be understood as describing what happened, rather than as naming a person, place, or object.

It appears twice in the Old Testament corpus: in 2 Chronicles 13:19 and Nehemiah 12:39. Since no explicit definition is preserved here, its ordinary lexical value is the name “Jeshanah.” The surrounding passages determine what is being said about that location, but the word itself functions as its identifying name.

This Hebrew word means “gather.” It functions as a verb, describing the act of bringing people or things together into one place or group. e.t: “Ashtaroth” is a proper name for a named entity referred to in the Hebrew Old Testament. It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word with a translated definition. The name occurs 12 times, each in a distinct verse, from Deuteronomy through 1 Chronicles. In several recorded passages, people speak about Ashtaroth and are described in relation to serving it, showing that the name identifies an object of religious devotion rather than a general action or quality. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on that passage’s wording and context.

Pekahiah is a Hebrew personal name, referring to a particular individual rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. It is rendered “Pekahiah” and appears three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in 2 Kings 15. The passages identify this person in connection with his reign and with the people associated with him. Because no separate definition or gloss is provided, the supported meaning is the personal name itself, “Pekahiah,” rather than an expanded interpretation of its parts.

Zuriel is a personal name, referring to one individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Numbers 3:35, and is rendered “Zuriel.” Because it is a proper name, its ordinary biblical function is to identify a person; the name itself does not provide a general teaching or concept apart from the person it names. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person’s role there.

The word means “first.” It describes something placed before others in an order or sequence, identifying priority or precedence rather than naming an object by itself. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Daniel 7, and each recorded rendering is “first.” Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic sense remains a designation of what comes first.

This Hebrew word refers to destruction—the destructive force or ruin that brings harm and devastation. It is used three times in the Hebrew Scriptures, each time describing something destructive rather than an ordinary difficulty or loss. Its renderings include “destruction” and “destroying,” showing that it can point either to the ruin itself or to the destructive action producing it. The word appears in Deuteronomy, Psalms, and Isaiah, where its surrounding wording connects it with severe forces that overwhelm or bring judgment.

This Hebrew word describes something as “swift”—moving or happening with notable speed. It can characterize a person, movement, or action, so its precise force depends on what it describes in the sentence. The word occurs 13 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, where its central idea remains speed rather than weight, size, or importance. Its established rendering is “swift,” which best captures its ordinary meaning.

This Hebrew word describes something "burnished"—bright, smooth, and shining as though highly polished. It functions as a descriptive word for a surface or appearance that reflects light. In the Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Ezekiel 1:7 and Daniel 10:6, describing the visible appearance of something gleaming. Its central idea is not merely brightness, but a notable brightness associated with a polished or refined surface.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “fourth,” identifying something as fourth in an order or sequence. It functions as an ordinal description rather than naming an object by itself. In its two Old Testament occurrences, it marks a position in the sequence: one occurrence is in Numbers 23:10 and the other in 2 Kings 6:25. The surrounding verse determines what is being counted or ordered, but the word itself contributes the clear idea of being fourth.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “womb,” referring to the place within a woman where a child develops before birth. It is used for the mother’s womb and can also appear in statements about children coming from or being given through the womb. The word occurs 26 times in the Old Testament, including passages about conception, birth, the firstborn, and the womb as a place of life and loss.

e.t: This word means “allowance”: a portion or provision given to someone for continued support. In its six Old Testament occurrences, it refers to food or sustenance supplied regularly rather than to a single gift. It functions as something received, especially in settings where a person is maintained by another’s provision. Its use in Proverbs and in the accounts concerning Judah’s exiles shows that the word can describe an everyday food allowance as well as an appointed personal provision.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to the broad expanse stretched out above the earth, commonly rendered "firmament" or "expanse." It is used especially in the creation account for the space associated with the sky and heavenly lights, and later in visions and prophecy for the vast heavenly scene. The word occurs 17 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its central idea remains a visible, extended space above rather than a specific object or person.

Shedeur is a personal name, referring to a specific man rather than describing an object, action, or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears five times, all in Numbers, and English renderings preserve it as “Shedeur.” The word’s role is therefore to identify a person. No additional ordinary meaning is established for the name itself by the available lexical information.

e.t: The word means “Shilonite.” It is a Hebrew designation used for a person associated with Shiloh, functioning as a descriptive name rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears six times, including references involving Ahijah and other people identified by this designation. Its use marks a person’s connection or identity in relation to Shiloh.

This Hebrew word means “have.” It functions as a verb, stating that someone has something or holds a position or power. In its seven Old Testament occurrences, all in Daniel, it appears in statements concerning rulers, authority, and what a person has. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary sense centers on having or holding something. The word occurs from Daniel 2:38 through Daniel 6:24.

e.t: This Hebrew word expresses being “named”—the identifying name associated with a person, place, or thing. It functions as a noun in Old Testament sentences, referring to a name as it is given, spoken, remembered, or connected with someone. Its 864 occurrences show that this is a broad and recurring biblical idea, appearing from Genesis through Malachi. The precise force in any verse depends on how the surrounding sentence uses the name. (Gen. 2:11; 1 Sam. 7:12)

This Hebrew word means “left.” It functions as a directional term, describing a position or movement toward the left side. In the Old Testament, it appears five times across five verses, so its basic sense is consistent but its precise grammatical role depends on the sentence where it occurs. It is found from Genesis through Ezekiel, including passages where it helps distinguish one direction or side from another.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “byword”: a person or people made into a widely repeated saying or example in public speech. It refers to a name or condition that others talk about, so that someone becomes known as a standing illustration of what has happened. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs four times, in Deuteronomy, 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, and Jeremiah. Its use in these passages presents a people as becoming a recognized saying among others.

This Hebrew verb describes being “guilty”—being answerable for wrongdoing or a trespass. It can identify a person or community as liable because of sin, including wrongdoing that requires acknowledgment and response. The word occurs 35 times in the Hebrew Bible corpus, especially in passages addressing sin, responsibility, and judgment. Its central sense remains the condition of guilt rather than merely the act that caused it. Context determines whether the word describes an individual’s guilt or the guilt of a larger community.

This Hebrew word means “wanton.” It functions as a predicate, describing the conduct or manner associated with the person or people being discussed. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 3:16, and its exact force there belongs to that passage’s wider sentence and context. The available English rendering presents the word as a description rather than an object or action.

This word means “warp,” the lengthwise threads that form part of woven cloth. It is a noun referring to a material feature of fabric, especially when describing cloth examined for a spreading or persistent defilement. The word occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within Leviticus 13, where it is mentioned alongside other parts of garments and woven material. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding instructions.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Psalm 39:10. Since the surrounding verse text and a fuller lexical definition are unavailable here, its particular force cannot be described safely beyond this restrained statement. The reference identifies its sole occurrence, but does not by itself establish the word’s precise meaning or the lesson conveyed in that passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “wine,” referring to the drink made from grapes. It is used of wine as part of the land’s produce and as something given, gathered, received, or enjoyed. The word occurs 38 times in the Old Testament corpus, from Genesis through Zechariah. Its uses include offerings and tithes brought before God, as well as wine associated with abundance and the good gifts of the land.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “increase.” It refers to an added amount, especially when something grows beyond its original measure. In the Old Testament, it is used in discussions involving money, lending, and the accumulation of additional value. The word occurs seven times, across six verses, from Leviticus through Ezekiel, showing a focused use connected with financial increase rather than a broad range of unrelated meanings.
